rv.q: It deserves more drama, emotion and political complexity on the ground.

The real takeaway is that a London theatre can, and does, dare to stage a new play about an important lesson from the past celebrating bold, risky international cooperation at a time when such courage has never been more required.

The set establishes a clear and divided world. On the left-hand side of the stage is a 1990s office environment, complete with the oldest-looking laptop I’ve ever seen, and a retro radio that occasionally blasts out news reports containing harrowing details.
In these dark days, a must-see.

Perhaps the start of something very exciting – an interesting, insightful voice, brought together well with a standout design team and exciting cast - but just not necessarily told by the most important voice in the room.
There's a dramatic punch to this play which lingers quite a while after you leave the theatre.

cn.t: This debut play about 1991's Operation Safe Haven brings insider authenticity to an under-reported humanitarian crisis, but critics find it struggles with didactic dialogue and lacks the dramatic punch and emotional complexity the subject deserves.
